The post WEEKEND READING: Why England cannot afford to lose its international Modern Languages Teachers appeared first on HEPI.
full_text:
This blog was kindly authored by Juliette Claro, senior lecturer in Education at St Mary’s University. Co-founder and co -chair of the UCET Special Interest Group for Supporting International Trainee Teachers and the Association for Language Learning Special Interest Group for Creativity in the MFL classroom.

England’s Modern Languages (ML) teacher supply is at a critical juncture. Despite decades of concern about the domestic pipeline, the system is now facing additional challenges. International trainee teachers are often native speakers or fluent in the language they teach, and frequently have extensive teaching experience in their home countries or internationally. But in 2025-2026 many have struggled to secure roles in schools.

The complexity and costs of the visa sponsorship for schools make up one aspect of the puzzle, but international languages trainee teachers have also fallen into a perfect storm of curriculum changes and financial pressures on schools. At precisely the moment when schools need subject specialists most, the system is making it harder for them to stay (Claro, 2025) resulting in more pressure on Initial Teacher Education providers to justify their employment rates post-graduation.

The reasons why international ML trainees are finding it increasingly difficult to enter the profession after completing their training in England are complex. All of them are intrinsically linked with the status of languages in the current curriculum landscape in England, the ever-changing immigration rules and a lack of national strategy to secure language specialists and linguists in the future economy.

As we are start a new academic year, let’s reflect on the challenges our international teachers faced in 2025-2026 and explore the potential solutions for the new academic year for the international students who secured places on the teacher training courses before the government changes in bursary funding.

The cost and administrative burden of visa sponsorship

The first barrier for international trainee teachers to secure a job is financial. For a school to sponsor a Skilled Worker visa, the average cost is around £2,000 per teacher, once the Immigration Skills Charge, Certificate of Sponsorship and legal/administrative costs are factored in. Despite being cheaper than some recruitment agency fees, for many schools operating under severe budget pressures this is still unaffordable.

But this sits uneasily alongside the reality that England does not have a domestic workforce capable of meeting the demand. The DfE Initial Teacher Training Census data consistently shows that ML recruitment targets have been missed for more than a decade, and National Foundation for Education Research (NFER) analysis confirms that languages remain one of the subjects with the most acute and persistent shortages. The improvement in recruitment predicted for 2026-2027 is not necessarily related to the fact that posts have been filled, but rather to a change in Languages provisions in schools, as explored later in this article.

In April 2026, the All-Party Parliamentary Group (APPG) hosted a roundtable discussion at the Houses of Parliament with our UCET SIG members. Facilitated by Darren Paffey, Labour MP for Southampton, and Baroness Coussins, the session explored the situation with sector leaders from Initial Teacher Education providers, Headteachers, International trainees and Early Career Teachers. Supported by professional associations such as the Association for Language Learning and the Institute of Physics, the group called for a three‑year visa for shortage subject teachers, which would align with the Initial Teacher Training Core Content Framework (ITTECF, DfE, 2024). The current immigration legislation is simply not fit for purpose and unethical for trainee teachers who come to train in UK universities at extreme costs but struggle to secure a job once they graduate.

Members of the UCET Special Interest Group in Supporting International Trainee Teachers reported a number of international trainee teachers being turned down for Early Career Teacherroles in schools because of their immigration status with non-specialists were prioritised over them to avoid the visa sponsorship burden. To support school leaders navigating the visa sponsorship, the Department for Education offered a webinar on 2 July to clarify the process with schools. Even though the webinar came late in the recruitment cycle, there is hope from the SIG members that this may support future recruitment of international trainees and ease pressures on ITE providers’ job conversion rates. However, without financial support to schools, international PGCE students will continue to struggle to secure the Skilled Worker Visa on their first post in a market already saturated with international Early Career Teacherstrying to secure their second year and a potential sponsorship.

A saturated job market for international Early Career Teachersplumbing future recruitment for ITE providers

The second challenge lies in the shifting labour market. International trainees who completed their PGCE in the summer of 2026 entered a job marketsaturated with international Early Career Teachers who graduated the summer before and who were also looking for jobs. Many of these visa holders Early Career Teachershold Graduate Visas (which are free for schools, but expire after 24 months). Most were offered one‑year contracts in September 2025, yet their renewal remains uncertain as schools cannot afford the costs associated with sponsoring Skilled Worker Visas, despite having invested significantly in their induction and development. The result is a churn of highly skilled linguists who wish to teach in English schools and build sustainable careers, but are prevented from doing so by current immigration rules.

The impact of changes to EBacc accountability, shift in Languages offer and demographics

With the EBacc ambition no longer requiring schools to encourage between 70 to 90% of pupils to study a language, the rising and unfunded costs linked to pensions, and inflation pay awards, and the recent fall in numbers of students entering secondary schools many school leaders had no choice but to restructure their curriculum offer and staffing. Despite the recent changes in Progress 8 measures, where languages are still required to meet the Ofsted dashboard criteria, some schools opted to reduce their languages offer to mitigate financial pressures. As shown in the latest Teacher Tapp 2026 for Schools Week. 29 per cent of respondents to the survey reported cutting down on language provision in their school setting.

The 2026 GCSE provisional entries are already showing a decrease in entries in French GCSE with a small rise in Spanish and German. As HEPI’s CEO Nick Hillman highlights in his report in July 2026, the top of the league tables for languages provision in English schools are in faith, selective or independent settings. This risks reinforcing the notion that Languages are an elite subject. The review of Languages provisions in schools will only worsen the future pool of linguists willing to study languages at higher education and consequently enrol in teacher training courses in the future.

As schools are trying to keep their books in order by cutting languages hours in their curriculum or by reducing their languages provision, the employment of ML PGCE graduates becomes more precarious. This disproportionately affected international trainees this year, who were already disadvantaged due to visa sponsorship costs. Members of the UCET Special Interest Group for Supporting International Teachers reported a noticeable fall in ML recruitment this year, mirroring the DfE and Gatsby Foundation’s latest data, ML job advertisements and recruitment were at their lowest levels in decades in spring 2026.

While the ethical dilemmas surrounding the growing number of PGCE graduates entering the new academic year without employment cannot be ignored, Initial Teacher Education providers are increasingly having to explain the reasons behind falling employment rates. Although Ofsted (2020) acknowledges that completion and employment figures are not reliable indicators of Initial Teacher Education quality, employment outcomes nonetheless remain central to future recruitment and to the public reputation of providers. In a turbulent and overstretched education sector, applicants may misinterpret a decline in job‑conversion rates as evidence of weaker provision, rather than recognising it as a symptom of wider systemic instability

A shrinking higher‑education pipeline

The British Academy Report on Inequalities in higher education offer across England highlights significant regional inequalities or ‘cold spots’ in access to language study, with many areas offering limited or no post‑16 provision. In 2025, 6,858 students took A‑level French, 8,325 in Spanish and only 2,224 in German. Even if every one of those students chose to study languages at university, there is a chance that they would have struggled to secure a place on existing courses across the country. University language departments have closed at an alarming rate over the last five years. As the new 2028–29 curriculum approaches and the pipeline of domestic languages teachers is shrinking, the question becomes unavoidable: where will the future domestic workforce of linguists come from if we continue to undervalue the expertise of our international workforce?

Why international teachers matter

As an international educator myself, I appreciate the contribution international teachers make through linguistic authenticity, cultural and grammatical expertise, creative and engaging pedagogies, but also supporting the diversity of pupils in English schools to feel represented. The Association for Language Learning Creativity in ML SIG has found that teachers teaching out of their subject specialism may feel less confident using authentic resources or designing creative, culturally rich lessons. Languages have the highest number of teachers teaching outside of their specialism (based on DfE data wehere teachers record on census having an A Level or degree in their subject(s) of specialism). This highlights the urgent need for more specialist languages teachers.

Whichever way we choose to look at this data, international teachers bring precisely the expertise that students need. Yet, as Panford (2026) warns in Languages, Society and Policies, we must guard against interest convergence. International teachers, especially international teachers of colour, should not just be welcomed in the country only when it is convenient and filling a gap in shortages. Although offers are related to demand, recognising the expertise and identities of international teachers as an integrated part of the teaching workforce is essential. International teachers deserve to be valued, to be financially and administratively supported and integrated as full members of the profession.

A system at a crossroads

Without international teachers, England will struggling to secure the future of Modern Languages in our schools. As numbers of A Level students in languages decline year on year, and universities close their languages and cultures courses, it is becoming increasingly difficult to study languages post-16 in English universities. As Stefan Collini reminds us of the dire financial state of UK Universities, the financial decisions to cut non-profitable languages courses in universities will inevitably impact the next generation of languages teachers in England in the next 10 years. If we are serious about fostering a love of languages in English schools, the recruitment of international specialist teachers becomes an essential key to that long-term strategy.

Breaking the cycle of languages being an elitist subject requires bold thinking and decision-making from our leaders. Recognising immigration as a force rather than a challenge would be the start of a truly inclusive society where internationals are valued and integrated from training to employment. Learning from other countries’ approaches international teacher recruitment may help us solve this puzzle.

title: 'We were just teenagers' - women abused while babysitting
summary: Midlands Correspondent Sinéad Hussey interviews three of the women who were abused by two brothers from Co Westmeath and their 30-year journey to justice.
full_text:
On 27 July last, two brothers from the midlands who sexually assaulted teenage girls in the mid-1990s were identified for the first time.

John (Johnny) Owens, aged 72, with an address at Cois Abhainn, Multyfarnham, Co Westmeath, was jailed last February for eight years.

He pleaded guilty to nine counts of sexual assault of three teenage girls, Deirdre Boyhan, Sinéad Nally and Aoife O'Dwyer, on dates between July 1992 and November 1996.

He could not be identified at the time because his brother, Martin Owens, aged 66, was facing trial for sexual assaults of Deirdre Boyhan as well as her sister Lorraine Kiernan.

In April, Martin Owens of Greenville, Dublin Road, Castlepollard, Co Westmeath, pleaded guilty at the Central Criminal Court to sexually assaulting Deirdre Boyhan and Lorraine Kiernan on dates in 1994 and 1996.

In July, he pleaded guilty to four more counts of sexually assaulting Deirdre Boyhan on dates in 1994 and 1995.

He was jailed for five years.

The court heard the women were aged 14 to 17 and were babysitting when the abuse happened.

Three of the women - Deirdre Boyhan, Aoife O'Dwyer and Sinéad Nally - spoke to Midlands Correspondent Sinéad Hussey about the two predator brothers and their 30-year journey to justice.

In early May 2023, Deirdre Boyhan sat in the cathedral across from Mullingar Garda Station, clutching a bottle of Rescue Remedy.

For 30 years, she had been hiding from the past.

But something had changed within her, and she knew that this secret which she had kept buried for so long, had to be told.

"I just thought, I have to do this. I'm going to walk across the road, and I am going to tell my story, and I have to let it take its course from there," she said.

At the counter in the public office, Ms Boyhan asked to speak to a detective and over the next few hours she recalled the horrific sexual abuse committed by Johnny and Martin Owens.

"It became overwhelming," Ms Boyhan explained. She was working as a special needs assistant at the time and "it took me completely by surprise".

"I was looking at these teenage kids, goofy and carefree, with not a care in the world.

"It became far more apparent to me how wrong it was, what had happened to me.

"I thought, I can't keep this in, I felt like I was trying to keep a balloon under the water," she said.

That May evening, inside Mullingar Garda Station, Detective Garda Adrian O'Reilly sat with Ms Boyhan and listened to her recount the abuse she had suffered.

She was just shy of 15 when the abuse began. It ended when she was 17.

"He was amazing. He sat me down and we spoke at length. He listened to my story, to what I was telling him," Ms Boyhan said.

She added: "He [Det Gda O'Reilly] was very understanding and caring and he explained how he was going to put me in contact with the Protective Services Unit.

'When she told me, I burst out crying'

Before reporting the abuse, Ms Boyhan had begun contacting other women who she knew had babysat for Johnny and Martin Owens.

What she didn't know was her younger sister, Lorraine Kiernan, had also been sexually assaulted by Martin Owens.

It was only during a conversation about the abuse Ms Boyhan had suffered and her decision to go the gardaí, that she found out about Lorraine.

"I didn't know about her until I spoke to her and told her I was going to bring this forward.

Watch: 'It wasn't actually my fault' - Aoife O'Dwyer

"We hugged and we cried and we're very close and people who know us as a family know that and I couldn't get over this," Ms Boyhan said.

Sinéad Nally, Ms Boyhan's neighbour and friend, also babysat for Johnny and Martin Owens.

The women know each other all their lives and their families are close.

Suspecting she too could have been a victim, Deirdre said she invited Sinéad over for a chat and a cup of tea.

"When she told me, I burst out crying, because I thought it only ever happened me," Ms Nally said.

She went on to explain how she then felt guilty because she had got the job for Ms Boyhan.

"When I left and went to college Deirdre took over from me, and I felt really bad, but I thought this was only happening to me, and it wasn't going to happen anyone else.

"You're only a child, you don't understand," she sobbed.

On 9 May 2023, Aoife O'Dwyer received a message on her Facebook messenger from Ms Boyhan.

When the message appeared on her phone, she knew exactly what it was about.

"Deirdre asked me to give her a call about something sensitive, and I knew straight away," Ms O’Dwyer said.

Becoming emotional, she explained, that like Sinéad, she thought she was the only one.

For years, the mother-of-two had kept what had happened to her buried deep within, blaming herself for the abuse.

"I developed very early; I was wearing a bra at 12. I blamed myself and I didn't think anything happened to anyone else," she said.

Watch: 'Free yourself from it' - Deirdre Boyhan

After the initial contact, it took Ms O'Dwyer some time to share her story with Ms Boyhan.

"I told Deirdre I was sorry it happened to her and that while he was a bit handsy with me, nothing had happened.

"After the call, I gathered myself and I rang my partner. When he got home from work that night, I told him about the abuse," she said.

For around three weeks Ms O'Dwyer said she put on a brave face to the outside world but inside she was crumbling.

"For 30 years, I always thought it was me, it was my fault, it was something about me.

"You have this secret and hope that no matter what, no one will ever find out.

"You become paranoid, you don’t like yourself, you feel disgusting. You just bury it and hope nobody will ever know," she said.

However, after speaking with her partner and her mother, Ms O'Dwyer decided to go to gardaí.

"When I started the process and spoke with Detective Garda Aidan Hynes, I began to realise, it's not my fault, I didn't do anything wrong.

"We were children, we were just teenagers," she added.

'Kings in their own castles'

At the sentencing hearing of Johnny Owens last February, Justice Eileen Creedon said he had targeted the victims.

She said his acts were gross violations, which took place on a continuous and extremely frequent basis.

The court heard that Johnny Owens would repeatedly molest the girls whenever he got them alone.

At the sentencing hearing of Martin Owens last month, Justice Tony Hunt said that he had groomed the girls and in the case of Ms Boyhan, plied her with alcohol.

He said Martin Owens was a trusted employer in a well-known local business who had engaged in the sexual exploitation of two children who had put their trust in him.

"You do feel vindicated and that was very important for us as a group. It took us a long time to find our voice."

He said these were not impulsive or youthful acts but were the actions of a mature person who would undoubtedly know what he was doing was wrong.

"When Johnny and Martin Owens were working and living their lives, they knew the indelible mark they had left and the untold harm they did," Ms Boyhan said.

Looking back now she said Johnny, who was married with children, was seen as a "decent fella".

"He didn’t drink a whole pile" and then "he’d drop us home, all the while he was trying to use us and abuse us," she said.

Ms Boyhan added: "Johnny in particular was well got. People loved the jack the lad way he went on.

"Unfortunately, some of us knew two sides of him and it was suffocating to keep that in.

"He was far too big of a character, and his brother was the same."

At the time of the abuse, Johnny Owens ran a successful business and provided huge employment in the area. Martin Owens, his brother, worked with him.

"This was the 1990s. There wasn't a load of money around," Ms Nally said.

She added: "In some houses, there were a few people from the one family working there so a lot of families were depending on them."

The women said locally the men were seen as pillars of the community, known for being hard-working and generous.

"They sponsored so many local teams, when money was needed, they did so much," Ms O’Dwyer said.

"They were definitely sitting as kings in their own castles, they were untouchable," Ms Boyhan said.

And so, for 30 years, the women said nothing, but all of them were struggling in their own way to deal with what happened.

When they decided to report the abuse in the summer of 2023, they knew a difficult journey lay ahead.

Women accused of 'doing it for money'

In late 2023, Martin Owens was arrested and questioned. His brother Johnny was arrested in January 2024.

When word of this began to filter through the local community, the women said they were subjected to false accusations, intimidation and hurtful comments.

"We live in a small community, everybody knows everybody," Ms Nally said.

The women said they were accused of "doing it for money" while others told them that because it happened 30 years ago, they should "let it go".

"People said these men are pillars of the community and look at the employment they gave," Ms Nally said.

"Basically, people thought because these men employed a lot of people and gave money to the GAA, they could do what they want.

"We were also told we were going to split the community over it," she added.

Even after the men were charged, the women said they continued to deny the allegations publicly.

In the pub and in the workplace, they made light of the serious allegations they faced, the women said.

Yet Ms O’Dwyer stressed that "both Johnny and Martin Owens pleaded guilty in court".

"All of that emotionally is crushing, absolutely crushing and you have to pick yourself up each time," Ms Boyhan said.

She added: "But the detective said from the start, trust the process and we had to trust the process."

Ms Boyhan said she was also questioned about why she took up a job at the business in later years.

She explained that it came about after she returned from college and she was offered the job following a chance meeting between her father, a family friend and Johnny Owens in Mullingar.

Despite her concerns, she said she "had no good reason to the outside world not to take the job", considering she was unemployed and this was a job that was well-paid, local and in her field of studies.

"I make no apology for working up there and I don't need to justify that; it was of its time," Ms Boyhan said.

Waiving their right to anonymity

On 27 July last, the women stood on the steps outside the Courts of Criminal Justice in Dublin, after waiving their right to anonymity.

The criminal case had concluded and both men were identified.

For the first time, Ms O’Dwyer said they all felt a huge weight lifted off their shoulders.

"I always wanted it in black and white, because so many people had doubted us.

"I believed if it’s printed and it's in ink; people can’t deny it. These men pleaded guilty to what they did, and people need to know that."

Ms Boyhan said the lid had finally been lifted on the litany of abuse carried out by the brothers.

She added: "You do feel that bit lighter. I watched many, many interviews with different people over the years, who have come forward and my heart would break.

"I used to be straight back there and think, would I ever be able to speak about it?"

With the court process now behind them, the women acknowledge the long-lasting impact the abuse has had on them.

Watch: Sinéad Nally discusses impact of abuse on school life

"We survived our lives for 30 years, not lived them," Ms O’Dwyer said.

She added: "We had to bring everything that we buried so deep down to the surface. You have to deal with it; there’s no burying it anymore.

"It affects everyone around you, you’ve to tell your family, your friends, your work colleagues and you are worried for them."

Becoming emotional, Ms Nally said she believes her life would have been different had she not been abused.

"I built a wall around me, and no one got in. Even when it came to partners, I had awful problems.

"I still have trust issues, and I never had children because I never met anyone until I was in my 40s. My life could have been so different," she cried.

Outpouring of support locally

The women said that since the publicity around their case, there has been an outpouring of support.

"We’ve been getting so many messages, people have sent cards and letters, some are from people we don’t even know," Ms O’Dwyer said.

She added: "I had a woman call into me in work last week and she said she has met me every day in work for 20 years and I’m always smiling.

"She asked me, 'how did I hide it?' But that’s what you do."

Ms Nally described it as putting "on a mask".

"I’ve had girls who went to school with me come up and say that I was always in good form in school, but that was all a front," she said.

Ms Nally added: "It’s like you overcompensate to make people think you’re really normal.

"It’s great to get the support now because we have been through the ringer with the attitude at the beginning when all this came out."

"You do feel vindicated and that was very important for us as a group," Ms Boyhan said.

"It took us a long time to find our voice," she added.

The women are now urging anyone impacted by sexual abuse to seek support, and they are hoping their story will show others that justice is possible.

"We found the Dublin Rape Crisis Centre brilliant, they were there for us throughout," Ms O’Dwyer said.

"If your case is brought forward and you end up in court, they are invaluable. We had no idea of the work they did, they have been incredible," Ms Boyhan added.

The women said they decided to speak out, not only for themselves, but for others.

"We’re very ordinary people but this is attainable," Ms Boyhan said.

She added: "From day one I said to the detective, I don’t have anything to lose. I came armed with the truth and that’s all we have.

"It is a slow process, and people are innocent until they are proven guilty, and we understand that.

"But if it is something that hasn’t gone away for you personally, speak to somebody, and free yourself from it."
